gist: Ed Yardeni and colleague Elias argue the post-midterm Nasdaq selloff is a buying opportunity in an earnings-led bull market with a compressed ~17x forward P/E, a 4-5% 10-year yield as the normal range, and a 7,900 S&P 500 year-end target. The labor market is a 'hire, no fire' economy (~5M monthly hires offset by separations) with no sign yet of AI job losses, and AI capex faces speed bumps rather than roadblocks.

themes.theme: Post-midterm Nasdaq selloff as buying opportunity

insights.claim: Yardeni views the sharp Thursday post-midterm selloff, led by the Nasdaq, as a buying opportunity particularly in technology, following his mid-September call to stay cautious until after the midterms.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Treat the post-midterm tech dip as a correction to buy rather than the start of a bear market.
insights.quote: it does seem to us that uh the Thursday selloff did create some good buying opportunities uh particularly in in in technology

insights.claim: Yardeni interprets the Wednesday rally immediately after the midterm results as short covering by investors who had positioned for a constitutional crisis that did not materialize.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Event-driven rallies may be positioning unwinds rather than new conviction; don't chase them.
insights.quote: We think that was a short covering rally on uh kind of people who had positioned for a constitutional crisis

insights.claim: Yardeni draws a 'deja vu' pattern: Nasdaq Composite plunges on Liberation Day and the Iran war (around March 30 and April 9) proved to be fabulous buying opportunities, and his most likely scenario is that the latest drop swings back up the same way.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Historical analogs of macro-shock selloffs in the Nasdaq argue for buying weakness.

insights.claim: The equal-weight S&P 500 and the Dow held up well and stayed above their 50- and 200-day moving averages while the Nasdaq Composite broke below them, and Yardeni argues such breakdowns are usually 'good drama' and more often just a correction.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Market breadth outside tech is intact; moving-average breaks in the Nasdaq alone are not a crash signal.

insights.claim: Yardeni's half-joking contrarian bottom signal is a relative who calls him asking whether to get out at bear-market bottoms; no call came last week, so he reads the selloff as a correction, not a bear market, and he also watches bull/bear ratios (Investors Intelligence on Wednesday and another on Thursday) that he expects to fall sharply.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Watch the upcoming Investors Intelligence bull/bear readings; a sharp drop would support a contrarian buy.
insights.quote: This is a correction not a bare market.

insights.claim: Transports have lagged, but Yardeni says falling oil prices improve the outlook for transportation stocks.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Lower oil is a tailwind for transports; a potential catch-up trade.

themes.theme: Earnings-led bull market and compressed P/E

insights.claim: Despite the Thursday selloff, the blended consensus S&P 500 earnings growth rate for Q3 increased because actual results came in stronger than expected (Yardeni cites AMD as a contributor), while the Q4 estimate slowed somewhat but remains very high.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Fundamentals improved even as prices fell, widening the gap that supports buying the dip.

insights.claim: Yardeni forecasts S&P 500 earnings of $425 per share for 2027 (consensus $426), $450 for 2028 versus analyst consensus near $500, and $500 only by 2030, arguing industry analysts, not Yardeni, are the most bullish on the street.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Expect downward revisions to 2028 consensus over time; Yardeni's 'permabull' label understates how exuberant bottom-up analysts are.
insights.quote: it's not us that are the most bullish. It's the industry analysts.

insights.claim: Forward earnings for large, mid and small caps are all at record highs, and Yardeni views the market as led by the level of forward earnings rather than its momentum (second derivative), though he notes the second-derivative approach of Nick Res has been successful.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Level-of-earnings framework stays bullish even if earnings growth decelerates.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 forward P/E has fallen to about 17 and change, below the Liberation Day and Iran-war lows and back to the 2024 correction level, because investors refused to chase the earnings boom; Yardeni doubts much more P/E downside.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Valuation compression amid record earnings creates an attractive entry point.
insights.quote: as earnings have soared uh the uh investors have said uh no no FOMO for us.

insights.claim: Semiconductors' low P/Es are a major reason the overall market multiple is down; Yardeni accepts the cyclical capacity-boom-then-price-bust argument but believes there is also a secular case for chips.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Cheap semis may be mispriced if the secular AI story outlasts the cyclical pattern; the cyclical-vs-secular debate is the key swing factor.

insights.claim: Yardeni reiterates a year-end S&P 500 target of 7,900 and welcomes a Santa Claus rally.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Positions for a year-end rally from current levels.
insights.quote: we've been talking 7,900 uh by year end.

themes.theme: Bond yields: 4-5% is the new normal

insights.claim: Yardeni argues a 4-5% 10-year Treasury yield is the normal range, as in the four years before the Great Financial Crisis, and that the low yields between the GFC and the pandemic were the abnormal period, so 'higher for longer' does not imply yields must come down.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Don't position for a return to sub-4% yields; anchor valuation models to a 4-5% range.

insights.claim: When the 10-year yield hit 5.35%, buyers started appearing around a 5% 'handle', leading Yardeni to think the worst of the bond selloff was over; he expects yields near 5% at end of this year and next, with buyers stepping in around 5.01%.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Treat ~5% on the 10-year as a buying level for bonds and a ceiling for yields rather than a breakout point.
insights.quote: A five handle was doing a good job of bringing buyers in.

insights.claim: The 2-year Treasury yield still anticipates about 50 basis points of Fed hikes, and the Cleveland Fed nowcast points to a 3% handle on October headline and core PCE deflators.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Upcoming PPI, CPI and PCE prints matter for whether the priced hikes materialize.

insights.claim: The recent drop in the 10-year yield came partly from TIPS yields and partly from a fall in the breakeven expected-inflation spread, which historically tracked oil closely; a large, volatile drop in oil and falling gasoline prices should lower inflation in a couple of months.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Falling energy prices are a disinflationary tailwind for bonds with a lag.

themes.theme: 'Hire-no-fire' labor market and AI jobs impact

insights.claim: The October employment report was strong and broadening: unemployment fell even as labor force participation rose, and average hourly earnings rose 0.4% month over month, with the prior two months revised higher.
insights.speaker: Elias Grienrog
insights.so_what: Labor data does not support recession fears; supports consumer spending and earnings.

insights.claim: Yardeni and Elias reject the 'no hire, no fire' label: JOLTS shows hires of about 5 million per month (5.4 million in September, not annualized) offset by separations of 5.3 million, so low net hiring masks heavy churn; they rename it the 'hire, no fire' economy because layoffs are just not happening.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Low net payroll growth is balance at full employment (~4-4.5% unemployment), not stagnation.
insights.quote: the net net has been looks like no hires, no fires, but that's not really what's what what's happening at all.

insights.claim: There is no evidence yet of AI causing widespread job losses; manufacturing added about 19,000 jobs in October, including roughly 7,000 in electronic and computer products and 7,900 in non-residential trade contractors, which Elias attributes to the data center buildout.
insights.speaker: Elias Grienrog
insights.so_what: The AI buildout is a net job creator for now; watch manufacturing and specialty trade employment as capex proxies.
insights.quote: clearly no no evidence yet of of AI causing any sort of widespread job losses.

insights.claim: Professional and business services employment surged in October, the strongest monthly increase since 2022 according to Elias.
insights.speaker: Elias Grienrog
insights.so_what: Counters the narrative that AI is already hollowing out white-collar hiring.

insights.claim: The private-sector employment diffusion index shows 60.4% of industries adding jobs on a three-month average, the highest since 2023 and in a solid uptrend, and the manufacturing diffusion index and ISM manufacturing also show signs of life.
insights.speaker: Elias Grienrog
insights.so_what: Broadening job growth reduces dependence on a few sectors and supports a broader equity rally.

insights.claim: Latest productivity growth was 3.4% quarter over quarter with modest unit labor costs, suggesting labor is not a source of inflation; Elias expects productivity growth to reach 4-5% in the 'Roaring 2020s' environment, while Yardeni is more conservative at 3.5-4%.
insights.speaker: Elias Grienrog
insights.so_what: Strong productivity supports margins and earnings without wage-driven inflation.

insights.claim: Yardeni says consumers keep spending because retiring baby boomers hold about $100 trillion, and he expects strong retail sales based on his earned income proxy.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Boomer wealth effect underpins consumer-facing demand.

themes.theme: AI capex: speed bumps, not roadblocks

insights.claim: Elias tracks three constraints on the AI buildout, political/social, financial and physical, and argues the political and financial ones now in focus will slow but not stop the buildout: speed bumps rather than roadblocks.
insights.speaker: Elias Grienrog
insights.so_what: Expect a slower, not collapsing, AI capex cycle; avoid pricing an AI bust.
insights.quote: they will put speed bumps sort of on the path of the AI investment boom, but they're not going to be roadblocks

insights.claim: Yardeni argues physical constraints (construction workers, land, permitting) would have slowed the AI buildout anyway, so political and fixed-income market pushback simply aligns spending with available resources, letting air out of the AI bubble without bursting it.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Slower AI capex reduces negative free cash flow and borrowing concerns, which is bullish for sustainability.
insights.quote: it's not like the AI bubble is bursting, but air is coming out of out of the AI bubble

insights.claim: Yardeni expects AI fatigue to help the rally broaden out beyond the AI trade as investors become less fixated on it.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Favor broader market exposure (e.g., equal weight) as leadership rotates away from AI names.

insights.claim: Rising Midwest domestic hot-rolled coil steel prices suggest data center construction is not coming to a screeching halt.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Use HRC steel prices as a real-time indicator of data center construction activity.

insights.claim: Responding to rumors that hyperscalers pay 15 times market price for data center land, Yardeni says it is unsurprising and simply raises costs and feeds negative free cash flow.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Land costs are another pressure on hyperscaler free cash flow.

insights.claim: Yardeni rejects a boom-bust scenario in which falling AI investment and stock prices drag down the economy, saying consensus worries about overspending, borrowing and excess capacity have been moderated by recent events.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A negative AI wealth-effect spiral is not his base case.
insights.quote: we're not in the roadblock camp. We're in the speed bump camp.

insights.claim: On software, Yardeni notes the market has already judged it more investable after the selloff months ago on fears AI would destroy the industry, and he suggests the only realistic way to play AI may be a broad tech fund such as QQQ because picking winners is too hard.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Prefer diversified tech ETFs over single-name AI bets amid hype and volatility.
insights.quote: maybe the only real way to to play AI technology anyways is uh to buy a um an ETF

insights.claim: Yardeni was cautious from mid-September partly because President Trump said he would re-escalate the war with Iran after the midterms; so far that bombing has not commenced.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Iran re-escalation remains a tail risk to monitor for oil and equities.

insights.claim: Food prices, as measured by prices in the Goldman Sachs index, may be coming down.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Another potential disinflationary input.
